Lucid Motors Got a Lifeline To Survive Long Enough for Its New CEO To Figure Out Automotive Business
8 photos
Photo: Lucid Motors
Lucid Motors reported the third-quarter financial results amid an operational reset under new CEO Silvio Napoli. The EV startup has reported a 30% reduction in cash consumption, while also securing $1.75 billion in funding from its Saudi investors. This comes in clutch as CEO Napoli admitted Lucid lost sales because they couldn't figure out "where cars were."
Lucid Motors reported another quarter of heavy losses , with a net loss of $831 million. Thanks to massive cuts and adjustments made since Silvio Napoli was appointed CEO in June, the cash hemorrhage was cut by 30%, to just under $1 billion during the quarter. All in all, a good result in the struggle to stay afloat and bring the Cosmos compact EV to market.
However, the biggest achievement might not be cutting losses, but getting new money to cover current expenses. Lucid secured another $1.75 billion in financial support from Saudi's Public Investment Fund (PIF), its majority shareholder. This comes after the startup raised another $1 billion in April, with $550 million coming from PIF.
PIF is estimated to own about two-thirds of Lucid Motors, and thus is very interested in not wiping out its investment. This explains why it continues to plug the company's holes with cash, even though it sometimes feels like throwing good money after bad. Besides investments, PIF has also offered $2.1 billion in loans throughout 2026. This raises the total funding and additional borrowing capacity to about $4.9 billion in 2026 alone.
This money makes Lucid Motors confident that it will have enough to fund its operations and investments into the fourth quarter of 2027. That should be enough to start Cosmos production, although its success is paramount for the company's survival. The time is also of the essence for the new management team led by CEO Silvio Napoli to get the ins and outs of running a car company.
That's not trivial, as Napoli himself admitted during the third-quarter earnings call. Lucid's CEO said that the carmaker lost sales over the summer, as the company "did not even know where the cars were." This caused significant delivery delays, which led to potential buyers walking away. For a carmaker with thousands of unsold vehicles that's struggling to survive, that's a stark admission.
Silvio Napoli promised this situation has been solved thanks to a new commercial team. Lucid now has better visibility on inventory and logistics and can better estimate when they can deliver the vehicle to a customer. In the third quarter, Lucid was forced to cut production to deal with the bloated inventory. Things should be much better in the fourth quarter.
How much better is anyone's guess. Lucid Motors builds excellent cars, even though they have sometimes been plagued by software bugs. However, they are expensive, luxury products, with prices in the upper five-figure territory, which explains the low sales. The low production numbers make it almost impossible for Lucid to sell its cars profitably. This should ease with the launch of the Cosmos EV in the second half of 2027.
